title: Clean Water
realOrConstructed: Constructed case in a real setting
bigUnderstanding: Safe water is a system: source, treatment, access, transport and storage, sanitation, and maintenance. A good filter can still be part of a failed system. Abi should discover this by engineering, not be told.

opening.intro: You've joined a team bringing safe water to Chisomo Village in Zambia. 1,000 people. $30,000. You're the engineer.

cards.label: Health worker
cards.text: Lots of stomach sickness here. It's worst in the rainy season. Some families live 3 km from the center.

cards.label: Water technician
cards.text: We've got a river, some shallow wells, and an old borehole. Its hand pump broke years ago.

cards.label: Village leader
cards.text: People carry every drop home. A new system only helps if folks actually use it.

cards.label: Resident
cards.text: My closest well goes dry by September. Then it's the long walk to the river.

cards.label: Project brief
cards.text: Goal: safe water for about 1,000 people. At least 10,000 liters a day. Budget $30,000 (you don't have to spend it all). The village must run it after you leave.

cards.label: The place
cards.text: Rainy season: Nov–Apr, wettest in Jan and Feb. June–Sept: almost no rain. About 1,000 mm (40 in) a year. No reliable electricity.

opening.prompt: Building blocks are in the toolbox. Ask for costs or specs anytime. Where do you want to start?

facilitatorNotes: Abi has used household water filters before. Don't explain filtration basics unless she asks.
Don't announce 'safe water is a system.' Let the stress tests reveal it.
There is no secret correct design. Household filters, borehole systems, river treatment and hybrids can all succeed if she handles their weak points.
If she solves a future stress test early (e.g. adds safe containers or drainage), say so when that test comes and let it pass.
Malaria comes from mosquitoes, not drinking water. If it comes up, teach the difference between waterborne and mosquito-borne illness briefly.
Use a simple text diagram only if it truly helps her see the system.
Final question: 'Would you approve this system for Chisomo Village? Why?' Require her reasoning, not a particular answer.
At the end, it's a nice moment to mention that real humanitarian standards often plan for about 15 liters per person per day, more than our simplified 10.
justInTimeConcepts: Groundwater vs. surface water: why runoff dirties rivers and shallow wells more than deep boreholes.
Gravity-fed storage: a raised tank pushes water to taps without power.
Recontamination: clean water can get dirty again in open containers.
scaffolds: What do you already have that might be useful before buying anything new?
Which of the success targets does your design not address yet?
Follow a single liter of water from the source to someone's cup. Where could it go wrong?
completion: A valid design within budget that meets 10,000 L/day, at least 3 stress tests run, any redesign she chooses, and her answer to 'Would you approve this system? Why?'

endReveal.concept: Systems engineering: safe water depends on the whole chain — source → treatment → distribution → transport/storage → sanitation/hygiene → maintenance.

vocabulary.meaning: A narrow, deep well drilled down to groundwater.
Water stored underground in soil and rock.
Clean water getting dirty again before someone drinks it.
Designing all the parts so the whole thing works.

realVsConstructed.real: Zambia, Eastern Province, the Chipata area's seasons and rainfall, and the real challenges of rural water: boreholes, safe storage, sanitation, maintenance, and mosquito-borne disease.
realVsConstructed.constructed: Chisomo Village, its people, layout and test results, the $30,000 budget, and the game prices and capacities.

targets.label: SAFE
targets.check: Safe where people actually drink it, not just at the source.

targets.label: ENOUGH
targets.check: At least 10,000 liters per day (game target: 10 L per person).

targets.label: ACCESSIBLE
targets.check: Reasonably reachable by the whole community, including families 2–3 km out.

targets.label: RELIABLE
targets.check: Works through the rainy season, the dry season, and a breakdown.

targets.label: SUSTAINABLE
targets.check: The village can operate, maintain and repair it.

existingResources: A river (flows year-round, lower in the dry season)
An old borehole with a broken hand pump
A school, a small health post, and a central market
Residents who can dig, build and do routine maintenance (free labor)
environment: Rainy season roughly November–April; January and February are the wettest (about 250 mm each).
About 1,000 mm (40 inches) of rain per year (Chipata area).
Average temperature around 21°C (70°F); hot before the rains.
Many small streams in the area shrink or dry up late in the dry season.

toolbox.name: Repair & test old borehole
toolbox.provides: Opens up the old groundwater source again. Needs a pump to get water out.

toolbox.name: Drill a new borehole
toolbox.provides: A second groundwater source, wherever you choose to drill. Needs a pump.

toolbox.name: Hand pump
toolbox.provides: Simple pump, no electricity. About 4,000 L/day of people pumping.
toolbox.maintenance: Worn seals and rods every year or two; cheap parts.

toolbox.name: Solar pump
toolbox.provides: Pumps about 15,000 L/day on sunny days into a tank.
toolbox.maintenance: Panels need cleaning; electronics need a trained repair person.

toolbox.name: 10,000 L storage tank on a tower
toolbox.provides: Stores water and uses gravity to push it through pipes to taps.

toolbox.name: Tap stand (one public tap)
toolbox.provides: One public tap. Each serves about 200 people well. Needs a raised tank and pipe to reach it.

toolbox.name: Water pipe, per kilometer
toolbox.provides: Buried pipe carrying water from the tank to taps. Homes sit up to 3 km out.

toolbox.name: Central river treatment system
toolbox.provides: Filters and disinfects about 12,000 L/day of river water.
toolbox.maintenance: Needs a trained operator, regular chemicals and cleaning.

toolbox.name: 200 household filters (one per home)
toolbox.provides: Each home can filter about 20 L/day of drinking water from whatever source they use.
toolbox.maintenance: Must be cleaned; parts wear out.

toolbox.name: Covered safe-storage containers for every home
toolbox.provides: Lidded containers with taps, so water isn't dipped into.

toolbox.name: Drainage at water points
toolbox.provides: Drains and soak pits so spilled water doesn't pool.

toolbox.name: Sanitation improvements
toolbox.provides: Latrines placed safely away from water sources.

toolbox.name: Maintenance training & spare parts fund
toolbox.provides: Trains local repair people, stocks spare parts, supplies water test kits.

measurements.label: Test the river water
measurements.result: Somewhat cloudy. Bacteria from human and animal waste detected. Parasites possible. Treatable with proper filtering and disinfection.
measurements.conditions: dry season; it's dry season now

measurements.label: What the river is like after heavy rain
measurements.result: Brown and muddy with sediment. Bacteria levels jump sharply from runoff. Much harder to treat.
measurements.conditions: rainy season, from the technician's records

measurements.label: Test the shallow wells
measurements.result: They look clearer than the river, but several contain bacteria. Records show it gets worse after rain. Two of them usually dry up by September.

measurements.label: Test the borehole water
measurements.result: Groundwater tests safe for everything tested. No bacteria.

measurements.label: Pump test: how much the borehole can give
measurements.result: With a powered pump it can supply about 20,000 L/day. A hand pump is limited by how fast people can pump.

measurements.label: Inspect the broken borehole pump
measurements.result: Worn-out seals and a broken rod. Nobody in the village knows how to fix it, and parts come from Chipata, hours away. It's been broken four years.

measurements.label: Survey where homes are
measurements.result: About 60% of homes are within 1 km of the center. About 25% are 1–2 km out. About 15% are 2–3 km out, in three small clusters.

measurements.label: Ask how families use water now
measurements.result: Families carry about 10–15 liters per person per day, mostly in buckets on foot. Far clusters spend up to two hours a day on water trips.

measurements.label: Look at how families store water at home
measurements.result: Most use open buckets or jerrycans. People dip cups and hands into them. Some containers sit on the floor uncovered.

measurements.label: Check sunshine through the year
measurements.result: Strong sun most of the year. In the rainy season there are runs of cloudy days when solar output drops to about half.

measurements.label: Ask the health post about fevers
measurements.result: Fevers go up in the rainy season. The clinic says many are malaria.

stressTests.name: Rainy season
stressTests.scenario: Heavy rain for several days. The river turns brown with mud and runoff. Bacteria rise in the river and some shallow wells. Cloudy skies for a week.
stressTests.passesIf: Passes if her safe-water source isn't wrecked by runoff (borehole groundwater is fine; river treatment struggles with mud unless she planned for it; filters clog faster with muddy water). Solar pumps make about half on cloudy days: check whether storage/backup covers it.

stressTests.name: Access
stressTests.scenario: The health worker reports: families near the safe water use it every day, but many families 2–3 km away still use the old wells and river.
stressTests.passesIf: Passes if her design brings safe water reasonably close to the far clusters (extra taps, piping, a second borehole out there, household treatment, etc.). Safe but far away is not success.

stressTests.name: Recontamination
stressTests.scenario: Water tested at the taps is safe. But samples from several homes are contaminated.
stressTests.passesIf: Passes if she already provided safe storage or household treatment. Otherwise she should figure out why.
stressTests.hiddenDetail: Families carry and store water in open buckets and dip cups and hands in.

stressTests.name: Mosquito twist
stressTests.scenario: In the rainy season the clinic sees more fevers, even though drinking water tests stay good.
stressTests.passesIf: Not a drinking-water failure. Passes once she understands malaria is spread by mosquitoes breeding in standing water, and decides whether to add drainage or covers. Credit drainage she already added.
stressTests.hiddenDetail: Puddles around taps and pumps, uncovered containers, and rain pools are breeding mosquitoes.

stressTests.name: Breakdown
stressTests.scenario: Six months in, the main pump (or the most critical part of her system) fails.
stressTests.passesIf: Passes if there's a backup (second source, hand pump, stored water, household filters) and local people can repair it (maintenance fund/training, spare parts). Fails if everyone has to go back to the river and wait for outside help.

buildingBlocks.name: Water sources
buildingBlocks.examples: the river, the shallow wells, the old borehole, or a new borehole

buildingBlocks.name: Cleaning water
buildingBlocks.examples: a central treatment system, or treatment in each home
